extracted.intended_audience: general American newspaper readership and policymakers
extracted.subtask_short: reporting on POW and internee treatment
extracted.subtask_description: A wartime newspaper report documenting alleged abuses, conditions, and violations suffered by American and Filipino prisoners of war and civilian internees under Japanese control during World War II. The piece catalogues specific failings (medical care, shelter, forced labor, executions, denial of rights) with illustrative incidents and cites the Geneva Prisoners of War Convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of adequate medical care
rubrics_metrics.description: Detaining authorities must provide sufficient medical treatment, medicines and hospital facilities to prevent avoidable deaths and treat diseases among prisoners and internees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘There is no doubt that a large number of these deaths could have been prevented had the Japanese authorities provided medical care for the prisoners.’ Examples: Camp O'Donnell hospital inadequate; American doctors given no medicine; quinine issued too late or in insufficient amounts; at Cabanatuan there was no medicine for malaria until five months after internment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate nutrition and prevention of deficiency diseases
rubrics_metrics.description: Prisoners and internees must be given a health-sustaining diet sufficient to prevent deficiency diseases such as beriberi, pellagra, scurvy and sprue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes widespread deficiency diseases and states this is 'directly due to the callous failure of these authorities to utilize the possibilities for a health-sustaining diet afforded by available local products.' Specific example: prisoners at Davao could see citrus trees but were not allowed to pluck fruit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate shelter, sanitary facilities and space
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding authorities must provide shelter, sanitary facilities, and adequate sleeping space to prevent overcrowding and insanitary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: 'many of the men had to live without shelter... Officers assigned to a shack 14x20 feet'; 'sleeping accommodations in a room intended for one person used by 20-30 civilians'; 'human excrement covered the whole area' at an overcrowded enclosure at San Fernando.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection from violence, torture and unlawful execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Detaining authorities must not subject prisoners or internees to beatings, torture, summary execution, or punishments greater than permitted under international law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report cites beatings with clubs, stones, shovels, golf clubs; bayoneting and shooting of those unable to keep up on marches; prisoners tied to posts and left for days then killed; imposition of death or long imprisonment for acts (e.g., escape attempts) where the Geneva Convention allows a maximum of thirty days arrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of forced labor without lawful basis or remuneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Prisoners, especially officers and civilian internees, should not be compelled to perform menial or punitive labor or be made to work without remuneration where prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Officers Forced to Labor' — officers compelled to scrub floors, clean latrines used by Japanese troops and work in Japanese officers' kitchens; civilian internees at Baguio forced to repair sawmill machinery 'without remuneration'; ten American engineers required to assist rebuilding military installations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for dignity and protection from forced propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Prisoners and internees must not be used for propaganda, humiliated publicly, or exposed to tours by civilians that violate their dignity and privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: American prisoners in Manila 'forced by Japanese soldiers to allow themselves to be photographed operating captured American military equipment' for a Japanese propaganda film; tours by Japanese school children, soldiers and civilians conducted at camps to 'satisfy curiosity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to the text of the Geneva Prisoners of War Convention and information on rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons held must be informed of their rights under international treaties and have access to translations of relevant texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report: 'No copy of an English translation of the text of the Geneva Prisoners of War Convention has been available to civilian internees or prisoners of war, nor have the Japanese authorities taken other steps to inform the persons held of their rights under the terms of the convention.' Reports that prisoners were told they had no rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to hold religious services and access to clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Internees should be permitted to hold religious worship and have priests or clergy minister to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the internees at Camp John Hay were not allowed to hold religious services during the first several months of the camp’s operation, and priests have not been allowed to minister to prisoners held by the Japanese in French Indo-China.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of canteen profits for prisoner benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits from canteens operated in camps should be used for the benefit of the prisoners, not appropriated by holding authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: 'In the prisoner-of-war camps at Hongkong the profits of the canteens have not been used by the holding authorities for the benefit of the prisoners.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of trade or access to private suppliers when safe
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible and safe, internees' access to trade with outside private suppliers should be permitted to improve food and supply availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report notes deficiency diseases are 'least in the civilian camps...where trade by the internees themselves with outside private suppliers is allowed,' implying such trade mitigates malnutrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and timely release of relief supplies and medicines
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief shipments (e.g., from Red Cross) and medical supplies must be allowed and not unduly delayed or inventoried in a way that prevents timely distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a shipment of medicines from the Philippine Red Cross was held up by authorities on the pretext they must make an inventory; 'they were so dilatory in doing that many deaths occurred before the medicine was released.' Also report of relief supplies piling up abroad because of diplomatic obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of basic household and food storage facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Detaining authorities should not appropriate essential household items (e.g., refrigerators) needed to preserve food and maintain health; adequate food storage must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: at Weihsien 'no refrigeration equipment was furnished by the Japanese authorities, and some... refrigerators of the internees were taken from them and were used by the Japanese guards, with the result that food spoiled during the summer of 1943.' Lack of sanitary facilities reported throughout camps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring humane transport and movement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When moving prisoners (marches, transports), authorities must provide adequate food, water, shelter and protection; avoid cruel assemblies or exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prisoners marched from Bataan to San Fernando without drinking water canteens; were assembled in open sun though shade was available; crowded transport with only twenty inches per man of sleeping space leading to deaths during transfer; many who couldn't keep up were shot or bayoneted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal application of humane obligations to civilian internees and POWs
rubrics_metrics.description: Both civilian internees and military prisoners are owed humane treatment obligations by the detaining authorities; differences in treatment should not absolve responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report observes medical care for civilian internees 'appears to have been better than that provided for prisoners of war, it still does not meet the obligations placed on the holding authorities by their government's own free undertaking and by the laws of humanity.' Specific examples cite inadequate care in camps in the Philippines, Shanghai, and metropolitan Japan.
